reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Characterised by opsoclonus (chaotic, involuntary, multidirectional saccades), myoclonus, and cerebellar ataxia
Behavioural disturbance, irritability, and sleep disruption are common, especially in children
In children it is strongly associated with neuroblastoma, so cross-sectional and metabolic tumour imaging is mandatory
In adults it may be parainfectious or paraneoplastic, notably with small-cell lung and breast carcinoma
Opsoclonus persists during eye closure and sleep, helping distinguish it from other abnormal eye movements
First-line immunotherapy uses corticosteroids or corticotropin with intravenous immunoglobulin, escalating to rituximab or other agents in refractory disease
In paraneoplastic cases, removal or treatment of the underlying tumour is central to management
reference.pathophysiology: Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome is an immune-mediated disorder affecting brainstem and cerebellar circuits that control eye movements and coordination. Loss of inhibitory control over the saccadic burst neurons, thought to involve dysfunction of omnipause and fastigial-cerebellar pathways, produces the chaotic saccades of opsoclonus, while cerebellar involvement generates myoclonus and ataxia. The immune response is frequently triggered by an occult tumour, classically neuroblastoma in children through cross-reacting antineural immunity, or by preceding infection; a defined single antibody is often not identified.
additionalDifferentials: Cerebellar ataxia of infective, toxic, or metabolic cause
Other paraneoplastic cerebellar or brainstem syndromes
Drug or toxin-induced ocular flutter and myoclonus
additionalInvestigations: Cross-sectional imaging of chest, abdomen, and pelvis to search for neuroblastoma or other tumour
Metabolic tumour imaging and urinary catecholamine metabolites in children
Paraneoplastic antibody panel in serum and cerebrospinal fluid
MRI of the brain to exclude structural and inflammatory lesions
Whole-body tumour screening in adults, including for small-cell lung and breast carcinoma
redFlags: Failure to identify an occult neuroblastoma or other tumour on initial screening
Severe ataxia or myoclonus impairing safety and function
Progressive encephalopathy or developmental regression in children
Relapse after apparent recovery suggesting undertreated disease or occult tumour
reference.prognosis: Many patients, especially children, improve with immunotherapy and tumour treatment, but relapses and residual cognitive, behavioural, or motor deficits are common, and outcome in paraneoplastic adult cases depends on the underlying malignancy.
pitfalls: Failing to search repeatedly for an occult tumour when initial imaging is negative
Mistaking opsoclonus for nystagmus or a functional disorder
Under-treating, as inadequate immunotherapy is linked to relapse and long-term sequelae
Overlooking behavioural and developmental effects that require broader support
